report.source_text: On examination, the patient had difficulty lifting the left arm, a left Horner’s pupil with mild ptosis and miosis, loss of temperature sensation on the right side of the body, and numbness on the left side of the face and right side of the body. The patient had a negative skew test and no swelling or trauma to the extremities. Deep tendon reflexes were absent in the lower extremities. NIH stroke score (NIHSS) upon presentation was determined to be a three (minor severity) based on left upper extremity motor drift and sensory deficit, and blurred vision (diplopia).

clinician.current_trajectory_hypothesis: The patient presents with acute neurological deficits highly suggestive of a lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg syndrome) based on the neurological exam findings (Horner's, crossed sensory loss). This clinical picture strongly points towards a PICA territory infarct. Brain MRI with DWI is the most sensitive imaging modality to confirm an acute ischemic stroke and localize it.

clinician.final_diagnosis: a 4 mm acute left lateral medullary infarct of the left posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) vascular territory
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 61-year-old patient presented with acute left-sided paresthesias, hemiparesis, difficulty moving the left leg, diminished sensation, ataxic gait, and left craniofacial pain. Neurological examination revealed left-sided weakness, left Horner’s pupil, crossed sensory loss (right body, left face), and absent deep tendon reflexes in the lower extremities, consistent with lateral medullary syndrome. An MRI of the brain confirmed a 4 mm acute left lateral medullary infarct of the left posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) vascular territory. CT angiography of the head and neck showed no large vessel disease in the head or intracranial stenosis, but confirmed 50% stenosis of the right internal carotid artery (ICA). A follow-up CT raised concern for an evolving right MCA infarct, but subsequent MRI confirmed no infarct in that region. The patient's left-sided mobility and weakness improved, and they were discharged home after four days on warfarin and meclizine, with recommendations for physical and occupational therapy.

Neurological examination revealed left-sided weakness, left Horner’s pupil with mild ptosis and miosis, loss of temperature sensation on the right side of the body, numbness on the left side of the face and right side of the body, and absent deep tendon reflexes in the lower extremities, with an NIHSS of 3.
MRI of the brain confirmed a 4 mm acute left lateral medullary infarct of the left posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) vascular territory.
CT angiography of the head and neck confirmed 50% stenosis of the right internal carotid artery (ICA) but no large vessel disease in the head or intracranial stenosis.
Patient's left-sided mobility and weakness improved to 3-4/5 strength three days after admission and was discharged on warfarin.
